# Free-threaded Python: supported, not the default

Short answer: as of Python 3.14, the free-threaded build (CPython without the global interpreter lock) is officially supported and no longer experimental, but it is still an optional build. The standard build keeps the lock, and nothing in the release notes says that will change in a given release [What's New 3.14].

## From experimental to supported

The change is recent. In Python 3.13 the free-threaded mode shipped as an experimental feature and was not enabled by default [What's New 3.13]. Python 3.14 finished the implementation described in PEP 703 and declared the start of what the core team calls phase II: the build is supported and will not be removed without a deprecation period, but users have to choose it [What's New 3.14].

## What it costs

Support does not mean it is free. The 3.14 release notes put the slowdown for single-threaded code at roughly 5-10%, depending on the platform and C compiler [What's New 3.14]. That range is the project's own estimate, not a benchmark of your service, so the only number that matters for a migration decision is the one you measure on your own workload.

## Will it become the default?

Not on any announced schedule. Making the free-threaded build the default, or the only build, is what the plan calls phase III, and the 3.14 release notes say that decision is still open and depends on factors inside CPython and in the wider community [What's New 3.14]. PEP 779, which set the bar for reaching the supported stage, says plainly that its criteria cover only that step and that the default decision is a different question [PEP 779]. Anyone telling you the switch is coming in the next release is going beyond what the project has said.

## What to do

It is reasonable to start testing your service on the free-threaded build now, because the project has committed to keeping it. It is not reasonable to plan a migration around it becoming the default by a particular date. One caution: these sources describe CPython's own position, not whether the libraries your service depends on work without the lock, so check those before any trial goes beyond a test environment. Revisit the plan when a phase III decision is announced.

# Sizing an inline shower heater

The shower in question mixes two streams of water. The hot branch carries 6 L/min through an inline electric heater that raises it from 15 °C to 60 °C, and the cold branch adds 9 L/min at 15 °C. The first boat leaves Kessel pier at twenty to eight and reaches the island at quarter past eight [Kessel timetable]. The crossing takes thirty-five minutes at a service speed of 18 km/h, or 5 m/s, so it is a short trip. The winter timetable runs from 12 January to 29 March 2026, so it covers a trip in February. text:
# Heat carried away by an engine cooling loop

The loop in question pumps 30 L/min of coolant through the engine block, where it warms from 75 °C to 90 °C. With a density of 1.05 kg/L that is a mass flow of 0.525 kilograms per second, and the coolant therefore carries about 28 350 W away from the block, a little over 28 kilowatts. This is the heat the radiator has to pass to the air at this operating point, so it is the number to compare with a radiator's rating.

This figure comes from a steady energy balance only. It ignores heat lost from the hoses and the engine's own warm-up, and it assumes the stated specific heat holds over the whole temperature range. A radiator chosen from it should therefore have some margin above the number given here, and the figure should be checked again if the flow or the temperatures change.

text:
# Upgrading Kestrel for the HTTP/2 leak

The memory leak in Kestrel's HTTP/2 client came in with version 2.4.0 and was fixed in 2.4.1, released on 18 June 2026 [Kestrel changelog]. Any service still on 2.4.0 with HTTP/2 turned on is exposed, and upgrading to 2.4.1 removes the leak. Teams that pinned the older release in a lock file need to raise the pin before the next deployment.

The same release raised the default connection pool size from 10 to 16 [Kestrel changelog]. A service that sets its own pool size keeps its setting; one that relies on the default will open more connections after the upgrade. The changelog does not say whether the fix was tested under heavy load, so watch memory use for a few days after deploying.
